title: Financial Sector Reform (Hayne Royal Commission Response—Stronger Regulators (2019 Measures)) Bill 2019
short_title: Financial Sector Reform (Hayne Royal Commission Response—Stronger Regulators (2019 Measures)) Bill 2019

speeches.speaker: Josh Frydenberg
speeches.brief: The government moved the Financial Sector Reform (Hayne Royal Commission Response-Stronger Regulators (2019 Measures)) Bill 2019 to implement recommendations from the ASIC Enforcement Review Taskforce, including strengthening ASIC's search warrant, telecommunications intercept, licensing and banning powers.

speeches.speaker: David Littleproud
speeches.brief: The government is implementing its response to the Royal Commission into Misconduct in the Banking, Superannuation and Financial Services Industry by extending unfair contract terms to insurance contracts (Schedule 1, recommendation 4.7), applying consumer protection provisions to funeral expenses policies (Schedule 2), and imposing a best-interest duty on mortgage brokers while reforming remuneration—including linking upfront commissions to drawn-down amounts, banning campaign and volume-based commissions, capping soft-dollar benefits, limiting clawback to two years, and prohibiting passing clawback costs to consumers.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: Labor supports the Financial Sector Reform (Hayne Royal Commission Response-Stronger Regulators) Bill 2019, which grants ASIC new powers to combat corporate crime, including enhanced search, evidence-gathering, licensing, and banning powers. The party criticises the government for delaying action on the 2016 ASIC Enforcement Review Taskforce report, which was tabled in December 2017 but not acted upon until now.

speeches.speaker: Jason Falinski
speeches.brief: The speaker moved the Financial Sector Reform (Hayne Royal Commission Response—Stronger Regulators) Bill 2019, arguing it strengthens ASIC’s powers to protect consumers. They accused the Labor Party of hypocrisy, claiming Labor’s past governance led to the Hayne royal commission and that Labor’s amendments and disruption of debate undermine consumer protection.
